title: The Cloudy Neonatal Cornea: Bilateral Haze Diagnosis & Management
summary: Bilateral corneal haze in an infant is an ophthalmic emergency requiring rapid differentiation between sight-threatening conditions like Primary Congenital Glaucoma, CHED, and metabolic disorders. Early intervention is critical to prevent irreversible deprivational amblyopia.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Urgency
sections.content: Bilateral corneal haze (congenital corneal opacity) refers to a loss of corneal transparency present at birth or within the first few months of life. It acts as a physical barrier to the visual axis, often leading to stimulus-deprivation amblyopia. Immediate referral for an Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA) is mandatory.

content.explanation: S: Sclerocornea; T: Tears in Descemet’s (Trauma/Glaucoma); U: Ulcers; M: Metabolic (MPS); P: Peters Anomaly; E: Edema (CHED); D: Dermoid.

sections.title: Primary Congenital Glaucoma (PCG)
content: Epidemiology: 1 in 10,000 live births; 65% male.
Classic Triad: Epiphora, Photophobia, Blepharospasm.
Pathophysiology: Maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork (Barkan's Membrane).
Signs: Buphthalmos (large eye), Haab striae, increased C:D ratio (>0.3).

sections.title: Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED)
content: CHED Type 1: Autosomal Dominant (Rare). Progresses after 1-2 years.
CHED Type 2: Autosomal Recessive (Common). Present at birth.
Genetics: SLC4A11 gene mutations (sodium borate cotransporter).
Features: Significant corneal thickening (up to 1000+ microns) without inflammation.

sections.title: Urgent Ocular Examination (EUA)
content: Step 1: Intraocular Pressure (IOP) measurement using Tonopen or Perkins tonometer (before general anesthesia deepens).
Step 2: Corneal Diameter (Horizontal/Vertical) using calipers. >11mm in newborn is suspicious.
Step 3: Pachymetry to measure central corneal thickness (CCT).
Step 4: Gonioscopy using a Koeppe lens to visualize angle structures.
Step 5: Fundoscopy (if view permits) or B-Scan Ultrasound to assess C:D ratio and axial length.

branches: Imaging: UBM (for iridocorneal adhesions), B-Scan (Axial length)
Labs: Urinary Mucopolysaccharides, Serum Cystine levels
Microbiology: Corneal scrapings if ulcer is suspected (TORCH titers)

sections.title: Red Flags: The 'Big Eye' Danger
content: Corneal diameter >12 mm before age 1
Asymmetric corneal diameters (>0.5mm difference)
New onset of clouding with irritability
Rapidly increasing axial length
Vague red reflex on Bruckner test

sections.title: Management of PCG
content: 1. Medical: Topical CAIs (Dorzolamide) or Beta-blockers (Caution: Timolol can cause apnea in neonates).
2. Surgical: Primary treatment is always surgical. Goniotomy (if cornea is clear enough).
3. Surgical: Trabeculotomy (if cornea is too hazy for goniotomy).
4. Refractory: Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD) or Diode Laser Cyclophotocoagulation.

rows: High risk of rejection in infants
Technically difficult but better survival than PK
Stable central opacity with clear periphery

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: CIGTS/AGIS principles: Aggressive early IOP control prevents 10-year blindness.
Endo-illuminated Trabeculotomy: Uses a micro-catheter (iTrack) to ensure 360-degree cannulation.
AAV Gene Therapy: Emerging research for SLC4A11 (CHED) correction.
Anterior Segment OCT: Now used intraoperatively to guide Peters anomaly dissection.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Normal newborn corneal diameter is 9.5-10.5 mm.
Horizontal Descemet's tears = Glaucoma; Vertical = Birth Trauma (Forceps).
CHED is often mistaken for glaucoma, but IOP and corneal diameter are usually normal.
Amblyopia management (patching) is as important as the surgery itself.
